name: Red Sweat Mystery
description: Eastern Airlines flight attendants have red sweat: complete KT Problem Analysis.

pre.proof:
Eastern Airlines flight attendants reported temporary red/pink staining on their face, hands and neck while in flight. Lead flight attendants, pilots and passengers did not report the same effect. Most cases occurred on Eastern A300 aircraft, with a few on other Eastern aircraft; none were reported on Eastern DC9s or other carriers. Symptoms began within about 30 minutes after takeoff and were short-lived.

Additional information: A300s replaced other aircraft on many over-water routes. Crews had been trained to demonstrate new life vests before A300 operations began in January 1980. Other new A300 materials included cleaning products, coatings, service-cart plastics and experimental air filters.
pre.healthy: Normal perspiration without red or pink staining.
pre.now: Red/pink moisture or marks appear on exposed skin during flight.

impact.now: Some Eastern flight attendants develop unexplained red/pink staining on exposed skin during flights. No inability to perform their cabin duties is reported.
impact.future: If the cause remains, further flight attendants may experience the same staining on subsequent flights.
impact.time: Before the next affected flight is the practical decision point. The case gives no specific resolution deadline.

ops.containDesc: Removing the new demonstration life vests stopped the reports of red sweat.

causes.accusation: Shed flaking red ink while handled during the safety demonstration
causes.impact: Red pigment transfers to working attendants' exposed skin and perspiration spreads it into apparently red sweat shortly after takeoff
causes.summaryText: Newly introduced demonstration life vests shed red ink on handlers; perspiration smears the transferred pigment into the reported red/pink spots. This is the historical confirmed cause from the separate post-exercise reveal.
causes.evidence: POST-EXERCISE REVEAL / historical case outcome (not starting evidence): Flaking red ink from new demonstration vests transferred during over-water safety demonstrations; perspiration spread the pigment. Reports stopped after the demonstration vests were removed. For teaching, distinguish the Most Probable Cause from confirmed True Cause. Confirmation options: verify which crews/aircraft handled the new vests; observe transfer during a controlled demonstration; conduct a safe materials-transfer experiment; or replace/remove the defective demonstration equipment and monitor for nonrecurrence. Only the historical removal/outcome is reported, not any live testing by this workbook.

what-object.note: Working attendants' vest handling explains their exposure, unlike pilots/passengers. Check whether the unaffected lead attendants did not handle these same demonstration vests; that role-level comparison is not fully documented in the learner facts.

where-location.note: Over-water A300 safety demonstrations give a specific path for vest contact and the A300 concentration; verify vest distribution on the few affected other Eastern aircraft and the unaffected DC9/other-carrier flights. Aircraft type itself is not a cause.

when-description.note: Vest contact occurs at the departure demonstration, then perspiration can smear deposited ink soon after takeoff; this fits the first-30-minute onset rather than requiring a later in-flight exposure. The separate historical reveal confirms the red-ink transfer mechanism.

causes.accusation: Left red-tinted residue on crew-contacted surfaces
causes.impact: The residue transfers to working attendants' exposed skin and becomes visible as perspiration spreads it
causes.summaryText: A newly used A300 cleaner might deposit transferable red residue on surfaces handled by cabin crew, becoming visible with perspiration.
causes.evidence: UNCONFIRMED learner alternative. No evidence in the available participant dossier establishes that a cleaning product contains red pigment, affects only demonstrators, or was used on all affected aircraft. Compare actual products, dates, surfaces and affected/unaffected flights before treating this as causal.

what-object.note: Requires working attendants, but not pilots, passengers or lead attendants, to contact the residue-bearing surfaces. The role/exposure split has not been established.

where-location.note: A300-specific cleaner might explain many A300 reports, but needs evidence that the affected non-A300 Eastern flights also used it and the DC9/other-carrier comparison flights did not.

when-description.note: Requires contact shortly before takeoff and red residue that becomes visible rapidly with sweat; neither the contact timing nor red-staining chemistry has been demonstrated.

causes.suspect: New A300 service-cart or rack plastics
causes.accusation: Released transferable colored residue when cabin crew handled service equipment
causes.impact: Color transfers to exposed skin during preparation and becomes visible as the crew perspire
causes.summaryText: New cart/rack plastics might transfer colored material to attendants handling equipment and appear as red spotting after departure.
causes.evidence: UNCONFIRMED learner alternative. An A300 equipment difference could generate a hypothesis, but the material must actually shed red pigment, and the hypothesis must still fit other Eastern aircraft, unaffected lead attendants, and onset timing.

what-object.note: Assumes only affected working attendants handled the residue-bearing carts/racks and unaffected lead attendants did not; verify actual handling roles.

where-location.note: Needs evidence of the same plastic on a few affected non-A300 flights but absence on Eastern DC9 and unaffected carriers; no such fleet inventory is supplied.

when-description.note: Requires handling the cart/rack before or immediately after takeoff rather than later during cabin service, plus evidence of red pigment transfer.

causes.accusation: Failed to screen ozone, producing an airborne skin reaction
causes.impact: Cabin-air exposure would supposedly cause red/pink skin moisture during flight
causes.summaryText: An experimental air-filter change might alter cabin air and cause a skin reaction, but this explanation conflicts with crew specificity and with the dated filter rollout.
causes.evidence: REJECTED by destructive testing and timing. Instructor guidance says the cartridges were still being tested and were not fully implemented until after the deviation began. A later rollout cannot explain the earlier reports, regardless of whether ozone could produce this visible effect.

what-object.note: A shared cabin-air exposure would not naturally explain why affected working attendants develop red spots while nearby pilots, lead attendants and passengers do not. There is no supported role-specific ozone mechanism.

where-location.note: Assumes the trial cartridges are unique to affected A300s and also somehow account for the few affected non-A300 Eastern aircraft; verify installations rather than equating 'A300' with a causal filter.

when-description.note: Cabin air would remain present beyond the first 30 minutes, while the deviation is reported only at early onset. More decisively, the filter implementation occurred after the problem started, so the dated Change cannot be causal.

items.summary: Compare life-vest demonstration exposure by crew role and flight
items.detail: Proposed confirmation of the remaining WHAT/WHERE assumptions: compare which working attendants and lead attendants actually handled the new demonstration vests; then map affected A300 and other Eastern flights against routes, DC9 comparisons and the demonstration-vest inventory. Preserve both IS and close IS NOT facts.

current-state: The red-sweat complaints stopped after the new demonstration life vests were removed.
what-changed: New demonstration life vests were introduced for A300 crews in January 1980.

notes.text: KT solution: Red ink flaked from new demonstration life vests and transferred to attendants during safety demonstrations. Perspiration spread the ink, giving the appearance of red sweat. Reports stopped when the vests were removed.

Key KT comparisons: flight attendants vs lead attendants/pilots/passengers; A300/affected Eastern routes vs DC9/other carriers; onset in the first 30 minutes. Distinctions focus on over-water routes and demonstrations; the dated change is the new life vests. Experimental ozone filters were not fully implemented until after onset.
